kilauea_notices.title: HAWAIIAN VOLCANO OBSERVATORY DAILY UPDATE
kilauea_notices.message: HVO Kilauea ORANGE/WATCH - Episode 56 lava fountaining occurred yesterday afternoon with fountains reaching 660 feet (200 meters), and the summit is now reinflating. The next episode of lava fountaining is likely several weeks away.
kilauea_notices.detail: Overview: Episode 56 lava fountaining occurred yesterday between 12:10 p.m. and 6:01 p.m., with fountains reaching about 660 feet (200 meters). The summit began reinflating after the end of the fountaining episode, and the next lava fountaining episode is likely several weeks away. Summit Observations: Precursory overflows from the north vent became more vigorous yesterday morning, building to a continuous low-level fountain in the late morning. This fountaining steadily intensified, and the onset of episode 56 was declared at 12:10 p.m. Fountain heights increased more rapidly after this time, peaking at about 660 feet (200 meters) between 1:30 and 2 p.m. The fountaining was limited to the north vent, with only some sporadic spattering seen in the southwest vent in the opening stages of the episode. Lava was carried from the north vent across the crater floor in several long channelized flows, as well as impressive sheet-like flows down the vent shield. Much of the western and northern portions of the crater floor were covered with new lava, with flows reaching into the eastern end of the crater. Fountain heights steadily decreased after 2 p.m. The fountain height fluctuated shortly before 6 p.m. and the fountain abruptly shut off at 6:01 p.m. Lava on the crater floor continued to flow over the next hour as the flows stagnated. Tiltmeter data indicate that episode 56 erupted approximately 8 million cubic yards (6 million cubic meters) of lava, with a peak effusion rate of about 690 cubic yards (530 cubic meters) per second, and an average effusion rate of 260 cubic yards (200 cubic meters) per second. Strong surface level winds from the northeast carried tephra fallout to the southwest, primarily into the closed area of Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park. As the eruption plume rose, upper level winds from the east and southeast carried the higher-level plume northwest towards Mauna Loa summit. National Weather Service radar showed the plume reached 18,000 feet (5,500 meters) above sea level. HVO geologists reported trace fallout of Pele's hair west of the summit on Highway 11 and the town of Pāhala. Seismic tremor increased rapidly during the lava fountaining episode, and abruptly dropped with the termination of fountaining. This morning, tremor remains elevated, with sporadic spikes that suggest gas pistoning cycles in the conduit. Only one small earthquake was located at the summit in the past day. Summit tiltmeters showed gradual deflationary tilt starting at about 8 a.m. Rapid deflationary tilt then accompanied the onset of fountaining. The Uēkahuna tiltmeter (UWD) recorded a total of 17 microradians of deflationary tilt during episode 56. Inflationary tilt resumed with the end of lava fountaining at 6:01 p.m. This morning UWD has recovered a total of 3 microradians of inflationary tilt since the end of episode 56. During fountain episodes, the sulfur dioxide (SO2) emission rate from the summit is typically 100,000 tonnes per day. Trade winds this morning are carrying volcanic gases southwest toward Kaʻū. Rift Zone Observations: Rates of seismicity and ground deformation remain low in the East Rift Zone and Southwest Rift Zone. SO2 emissions from the East Rift Zone remain below the detection limit. Analysis: Following the end of episode 56 on November 5, 2026, summit tiltmeters recorded a typical post-fountaining recovery, with a steady inflationary trend that continues this morning. Based on previous episodes, the next lava fountaining is likely several weeks away. Kīlauea has been erupting episodically since December 23, 2024, from two primary vents (north and south) within Halemaʻumaʻu at the summit. Lava fountaining episodes generally last less than 12 hours and are separated by pauses of two or more weeks. HVO continues to closely monitor Kīlauea and remains in contact with Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park and the Hawaiʻi County Civil Defense Agency regarding eruptive hazards. Hazards: Eruptive activity since December 202

mauna_loa_notices.title: HAWAIIAN VOLCANO OBSERVATORY MONTHLY UPDATE
mauna_loa_notices.message: HVO Mauna Loa GREEN/NORMAL - Mauna Loa earthquake counts were within typical levels in October, and minor inflation continues.
mauna_loa_notices.detail: Mauna Loa had a slight increase in seismic activity compared to the previous month; a total of 66 earthquakes were detected in Mauna Loa's summit region during the October reporting period, after 53 in September. These variations are within the typical range for the past two years. Most earthquakes occurred deep beneath the upper Southwest Rift Zone or broadly scattered around the upper flanks. Data from Global Positioning System (GPS) instruments on Mauna Loa showed slight inflation across the summit region in the past month. Oscillations between contraction and inflation patterns during non-eruptive periods are normal, but inflation has been the dominant trend since the 2022 eruption, consistent with magma refilling the summit reservoir system. Gas and temperature data from a station on Mauna Loa's Southwest Rift Zone indicate these values are at background levels, with little change relative to previous months. HVO continues to closely monitor Mauna Loa and will issue another update in one month, or earlier, should conditions change significantly.
